items.text:
Evolution is typically thought of as a slow, gradual process, with species adapting over generations in response to environmental changes. But when environments change suddenly and dramatically, evolution can happen much faster than scientists once thought.
On March 27, 1964, a powerful earthquake struck southern Alaska , lifting parts of the coastline and creating new freshwater ponds from what had once been marine habitat. Several threespine stickleback fish became trapped in these ponds across at least three islands in Prince William Sound and the Gulf of Alaska, forcing them to quickly adapt to their new and very different environments. Isolated from other stickleback populations still in the ocean, the freshwater sticklebacks developed dramatically in less than 50 years.
Scientists from the University of Alaska Fairbanks, University of Alaska Anchorage, University of Oregon, and University of Illinois compared the newly adapted stickleback with older freshwater populations and found that, despite being less than 50 years old, they had evolved many of the same genetic and physical characteristics, including differences in their eyes, body shape, color, bone size, and body armor.
“We find that the freshwater populations, despite population genetic analyses clearly supporting their young age, have diverged phenotypically from oceanic ancestors to nearly the same extent as populations that were likely founded thousands of years ago,” reported the scientists in 2010. “Our results support the intriguing hypothesis that most stickleback evolution in fresh water occurs within the first few decades after invasion of a novel environment.”
This incredible discovery suggests that rapid evolution could be possible in other species, too. “This research perhaps opens a window on how climate change could affect all kinds of species,” said Susan L. Bassham, a Cresko lab senior research associate who co-authored the paper. “What we’ve shown here is that organisms—even vertebrates, with long generation times—can respond very fast to environmental change.”

items.desc: A Canadian man is writing a coda into the lives of scrapped musical instruments by using them to offer a free lunch to his feathered neighbors. A nibble of corn or seed comes with no strings attached at the Frets and Feathers Cafe, run by retired teacher Rob Burke from Prince Edward Island. The former […] The post Retired Teacher Turns Retired Musical Instruments into Bird Feeders (LOOK) appeared
items.text:
A Canadian man is writing a coda into the lives of scrapped musical instruments by using them to offer a free lunch to his feathered neighbors.
A nibble of corn or seed comes with no strings attached at the Frets and Feathers Cafe, run by retired teacher Rob Burke from Prince Edward Island.
The former math teacher saw someone from Europe make an old guitar into a birdfeeder on social media and figured he could do one better: a three-course orchestra.
Asking for donations of broken instruments for an art project on Facebook, Burke was delighted to receive 6 guitars, an old violin, and pieces of a drum set.
He got to work attaching driftwood perches and metal feeding dishes into the hollow-body guitars.
CBC reported that his choice of a glue gun was just fine at first, but once the heavier blue jays began visiting, he had to reattach the perches and dishes more firmly.
His Facebook wall features an array of common birds, which Burke says he has taken a greater interest in since retiring. Videos are often paired with music, and make for great viewing.
He has since seen a woodpecker, corvids, and chickadees, and expects to see further species as the seasons change.
For any other PE Islanders, Burke welcomes further instrument donations to expand the Peck and Play Orchestra. One can contact him over Facebook.

items.title: 67 Fails, Funny Moments And Weird Takes That Might Make Scrolling Way More Enjoyable
items.desc: Sometimes, the funniest things are the ones people notice in everyday life but rarely bother to say out loud. From oddly specific observations and unexpected comparisons to familiar situations described in hilariously accurate ways, people online have a knack for turning ordinary thoughts into comedy gold. And there's a reason these jokes resonate so much: humor thrives on recognition, surprise, a
items.text:
Observational humor is built around noticing the little things people experience every day but rarely stop to think about. According to Psychology Today , this type of comedy takes familiar situations, ordinary behaviors, and small social absurdities and presents them in a way that makes people recognize just how amusing they can be.
Much of its appeal comes from the familiarity of the experience, especially when someone points out something that others have encountered but never quite put into words. However, simply describing an everyday occurrence isn't always enough to make it funny. The observation also needs an unexpected angle that encourages people to look at something familiar differently.
This kind of humor relies on a combination of relatable situations, precise details, and surprising twists. A comedian might start with something everyone recognizes, such as an awkward social interaction or a common daily inconvenience, before drawing attention to an unusual detail that makes the situation seem ridiculous.
The ability to notice these details is an important part of observational comedy, as even the smallest habits, contradictions, or unspoken social rules can become entertaining material. The more specific an observation is, the easier it can be for people to recognize the experience and appreciate the humor behind it.
Sometimes, the funniest jokes are simply ordinary situations described in a way that makes their absurdity impossible to ignore.
Beyond making people laugh individually, humor also has an important social function. Research discussed by the Greater Good Science Center found that sharing laughter can increase people's feelings of similarity toward one another, which can subsequently make them feel more positively about each other and more interested in building a connection.
This suggests that finding the same things funny can be more meaningful than simply enjoying a good joke. When people recognize the same absurdity or relate to the same everyday experience, they discover a small point of common ground that makes interacting with one another feel more natural.
This sense of connection can develop in several ways. Laughter can make unfamiliar social situations less uncomfortable, ease tension during difficult conversations, and help people feel more relaxed around one another. It can also create a sense of belonging when people develop shared jokes or recognize the same amusing details in their surroundings.

items.title: Texans Work for Free on Farms That Aren’t Theirs to Send Others’ Kids to College
items.desc: Texas residents are farming land that isn’t theirs for free in order to raise money to help send kids—who also aren’t theirs—off to college. As true to the spirit of Thanksgiving as anything you’ll read this week, the 15-year tradition has paid out $3 million in scholarships to hundreds of high schoolers. “We just treat […] The post Texans Work for Free on Farms That Aren’t Theirs to Send Others’
items.text:
Texas residents are farming land that isn’t theirs for free in order to raise money to help send kids—who also aren’t theirs—off to college.
As true to the spirit of Thanksgiving as anything you’ll read this week, the 15-year tradition has paid out $3 million in scholarships to hundreds of high schoolers.
“We just treat it like it’s ours—like it’s another one of our farms,” local farmer Derik Grotegut said, referring to the school district’s 640 acres where nearly 1,000 residents work pro bono on one crop of spring corn and one of winter wheat.
Rather than leaving it to family, friends, or a trust, the longtime landowner of those 640 acres left his Texas panhandle farm to the Gruver school district in 1984.
Described by the Washington Post, reporting on the tradition , as a farming community through and through, Gruver’s school district had long leased the farmland to generate income for higher-order school supplies like chemistry beakers and textbooks. It was about 15 years ago that schoolboard members decided to up the ante on their land substantially.
It would require some 1,000 local agriculturalists to make the plan work: an astonishing bet on the sense of commonwealth within the city. The land would be worked, and the crop sold to fund scholarships.
Students from the very beginning of their academic journeys would receive a briefing: excel in school, at volunteering, in extracurricular activities, and earn a bigger share of the crop profits to pay college. The program met with almost instant success, as the Post tells it, with the first decade seeing 48 children become the first in their families to attend university and each annual harvest yielded around $400,000.
MORE FARMING STORIES: Wind Turbines Provide Half of Rancher’s Income Since He Decided to Invite Them on His Land
“It is unbelievable, the fact that the community will be willing to do this,” Troy Seagler, Gruver High School’s former principal who helped come up with the idea, told the Post.
Farmers indeed volunteer their time, and a Gruver-based feed yard buys their crop at a premium just to swell the scholarship harvest. Meanwhile, 15 years after they started, Gruver grads are bringing their degrees back to town, opening businesses and taking positions according to their new skillsets.
Unsurprisingly, perhaps, many of those who’ve walked off with scholarships often return as farmers, to carry on at the world’s true oldest profession down through the century.

items.title: Severe Thanksgiving storms leave roads flooded and trees fallen
items.desc: Hundreds of thousands of people were without power after severe weather hit both coasts of the United States during the Thanksgiving holiday.
items.text:
Both US coasts have been battered by severe Thanksgiving storms, leaving behind flooded roads, fallen trees, and widespread power outages for hundreds of thousands of people.
Although the weather is expected to improve, hundreds of flights remain delayed or cancelled on Friday.
Beyond the travel disruption, impacts were widespread across the east Coast, and US President Donald Trump said he would consider releasing emergency funds.

items.title: 72 Clever Lifehacks That Might Make Your Everyday Life A Little Easier
items.desc: Why make everyday tasks harder than they need to be? These clever lifehacks offer simple ways to save time, avoid unnecessary hassle, and make your daily routine a little smoother. Pandas, scroll on; you might even find a trick you wish you'd known years ago!
items.text:
Life can be busy enough without making every little task harder than it needs to be. Sometimes, we get so used to doing things a certain way that we never stop to consider whether there's an easier approach.
This is why discovering a clever shortcut can feel like finding a secret level in a video game. It saves you some effort and makes you wonder how much time you've wasted doing things the long way.
There's actually a psychological reason why making tasks easier can help us get them done. Research on habits suggests people are more likely to repeat behaviors when there are fewer obstacles standing in their way.
When an action requires less effort or is easier to get started, we're less likely to put it off and more likely to follow through. Sometimes, getting things done has less to do with finding more motivation and more to do with removing unnecessary friction.
Practice also plays a big part in making everyday life easier. A study published in Current Opinion in Behavioral Sciences explains that repeating an activity helps people perform it faster, develop skills, and use less mental effort.
Think about how overwhelming something can feel the first time you try it compared with how easily you manage it after doing it several times. Your brain gets better at handling familiar tasks, leaving you with more mental energy for other things.
Having a routine is another great life cheat . When you connect an action to something you already do regularly, remembering to do it becomes much easier. With enough repetition, your brain starts associating certain situations with specific actions, so you don't have to think through every step.
This is closely related to muscle memory, which helps familiar physical movements feel almost automatic. In fact, a study published in the British Journal of Health Psychology found that linking a new behavior to an existing routine helped participants repeat it more consistently.

items.title: Ferrari Is Dipping Its Toe Into Ocean Racing With Its New 100-Foot Flying ‘Hypersail’
items.desc: Ferrari Is Dipping Its Toe Into Ocean Racing With Its New 100-Foot Flying ‘Hypersail’ Ferrari is synonymous with fast cars, but the company is expanding its fleet by dipping its toe into ocean racing. Hypersail is part of Ferrari’s ambitious move into this form of professional competition, building on its automotive engineering expertise and the demands of high-performance team racing. The Hypersa
items.text:
Ferrari is synonymous with fast cars, but the company is expanding its fleet by dipping its toe into ocean racing. Hypersail is part of Ferrari ’s ambitious move into this form of professional competition, building on its automotive engineering expertise and the demands of high-performance team racing.
The Hypersail is a 100-foot flying ocean monohull, a sailing vessel with a single hull that’s the primary way it stays afloat. Moving a vessel this size above the water requires enormous lift, balance, and speed. Ferrari’s groundbreaking technology is designed to lift the giant vessel off the ocean surface. The team aims to break records and technological barriers. The project has generated 20 patents designed to solve problems involving energy generation, sail handling, aerodynamics, and controlling a 100-foot boat traveling above the water.
The secret behind Hypersail’s ability to rise above the waves lies in three underwater components: its foils, keel, and rudder. Together, these appendages generate lift, maintain balance, and respond to changing sea conditions. The foils act like underwater wings, producing the upward force needed to lift the hull out of the water and reduce drag. The keel incorporates an additional foil with a movable flap that helps manage flight and provides another point of support. Meanwhile, the rudder features a small movable wing that continuously adjusts the boat’s steering.
Hypersail’s flight control system draws on Ferrari’s automotive electronic systems and dynamic control expertise. It automatically analyzes environmental conditions like wind and waves, along with boat speed and heel angle or tilt, to keep the boat stable and balanced no matter the sea’s temperament. This also frees the crew to focus on reading the ocean, making strategic decisions, and finding ways to maximize performance.
Additionally, the racing yacht is designed for energy efficiency. It generates its own electricity using renewable energy sources, including solar panels and wind turbines, for greater self-sufficiency on long ocean voyages.
One of the project’s major long-term ambitions is to set offshore records, potentially including an attempt at the Jules Verne Trophy, the record for the fastest nonstop, unassisted circumnavigation of the globe. The first launch and sea trials are expected in 2027.

items.desc: 167 years ago today, the British naturalist and geologist Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species explaining his theory of evolution. The first edition—which has been voted by publishers and librarians as the most influential academic book ever written—introduced the scientific theory that populations evolve over the course of generations through a process of […] The post Good News in Hi
items.text:
167 years ago today, the British naturalist and geologist Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species explaining his theory of evolution. The first edition—which has been voted by publishers and librarians as the most influential academic book ever written—introduced the scientific theory that populations evolve over the course of generations through a process of natural selection. It presented a body of evidence that the diversity of life arose by common descent through a tree-like branching pattern of evolution. WATCH an animation about how little finches were crucial to his discovery, and how pepper moths evolved due to pollution… (1859)
Darwin included evidence that he had gathered on expeditions to South America in the 1830s and his subsequent findings from research and experimentation, and showed how natural selection is a scientifically testable mechanism. Within two decades widespread scientific agreement solidified that evolution had occurred, and by the mid-20th century Darwin’s concept of evolutionary adaptation through natural selection became central to modern evolutionary theory—and the unifying concept of the life sciences.
Modern evolutionary theory continues to develop, but his writings still explain the diversity of living organisms and their adaptation to the environment; make sense of the geological record; and hold up under modern genome analysis.
Because of church teachings at the time, his theory was much maligned, but clergymen later came to accept natural selection, explaining it as an instrument of God’s design. The Vatican stated its official position in 1950, which held that evolution was consistent with Catholic teachings. Darwin, himself, believed at the outset that God had been creating life through the laws of nature.

items.title: 82 Urban Landscapes That Have A Rather Complicated Relationship With Aesthetics (New Pics)
items.desc: Modern development does have its upsides, but we can’t dismiss its uglier side. You can see it through the urban hellscapes many are unfortunately living in, and here are some examples. These photos, as depressing as they are, only prove that aesthetics isn’t a top priority for many urban developers.
items.text:
According to statistics , 100 million new road vehicles were sold worldwide in 2025. That means many places have prioritized automobiles. For community development planner John Guszkowski , this is one of many reasons many places have turned into urban hell.
“Even in existing, established cities, focusing too heavily on vehicles - parking lots, massive parking structures, core intersections that prioritize vehicle throughput rather than pedestrians - can degrade an urban environment,” he told Bored Panda .
Prioritizing tourism may benefit the economy, but Guszkowski says the drawback shows up in poor urban planning.
“Converting year-round housing to Airbnbs or tourist-friendly amenities can turn a vibrant community into a fake, Disneyland version of what that community used to be,” he said, noting how economic success can displace lower-income residents.
Many cities have also removed iconic landmarks that make their town unique. One prominent example is Chicago tearing down the monumental Garrick Theatre in 1961 and replacing it with a parking garage.
For S-Line Contractors project executive Fahed Bitar , tearing down these structures also makes a city much less aesthetically pleasing.
“The entire blocks that are being leveled and redeveloped previously gave the area its uniqueness and now will resemble any other block in any other city,” Bitar said. ‘
According to Bitar, buildings constructed with blank walls and neighborhoods with little to no green space also contribute to a city’s uglification.
Never miss a story that brings joy to the world. Add us on Google
So how should urban developers approach planning? Guszkowski says sustainability should be the utmost priority.
“Affordable housing is useless unless you have adequate sanitation and useful infrastructure, as well as nearby or integrated green spaces,” he said. “Places should be planned comprehensively. Don't expand road or sewer infrastructure unless what it is going to serve is properly planned for build-out.”

items.desc: Smithsonian American Art Museum Explores U.S. History Through 225 Photographs The Smithsonian American Art Museum brings together 225 photographs documenting the United States around its 1976 Bicentennial in Much Here Is Beautiful: Photography Surveys of the U.S. Bicentennial. Featuring work by more than 70 photographers, the exhibition spans the country, from New York City to rural Appalachia. To
items.text:
Robert K. Hower, July 4, 1976, Louisville, KY, 1976, gelatin silver print, Smithsonian American Art Museum, Transfer from the National Endowment for the Arts, 1983.63.789, ©1976, Robert K. Hower
The Smithsonian American Art Museum brings together 225 photographs documenting the United States around its 1976 Bicentennial in Much Here Is Beautiful: Photography Surveys of the U.S. Bicentennial . Featuring work by more than 70 photographers, the exhibition spans the country, from New York City to rural Appalachia. Together, these images capture communities during a period of social and economic change.
The photographs grew out of a federal initiative launched by the National Endowment for the Arts (NEA) to mark the nation’s 200th anniversary. Inspired by the Farm Security Administration’s documentary photography during the Great Depression , the program funded 72 regional surveys of American life. The exhibition reunites selections from these projects for the first time, including works rediscovered through curatorial research.
Much Here Is Beautiful also traces the history of federal survey photography. It opens with 19th-century images by Carleton E. Watkins, Timothy O’Sullivan, and William H. Jackson, whose photographs introduced many Americans to the West’s landscapes. Works by Dorothea Lange and Walker Evans show how documentary photography later expanded to record everyday life.
The exhibition spans four regions, from Lee Friedlander’s photographs of industrial towns in the Northeast to Robert Townsend Jones Jr.’s previously unseen images of Beale Street in Memphis. In the Midwest, Joel Meyerowitz photographs St. Louis and its Gateway Arch, while John Margolies documents the roadside attractions that define the American landscape.
In the West, Mark Klett and JoAnn Verburg revisit historic landscapes through their Rephotographic Survey Project, placing contemporary images alongside 19th-century photographs. Reagan Louie’s photographs of San Francisco’s Chinatown offer a more personal perspective on the communities and histories that shape the country.
The exhibition takes its title from Robert Hayden’s 1978 poem “American Journal.” The phrase offers a fitting lens for photographs that look beyond familiar national symbols. Instead, they document the people, places, and everyday experiences that shape American life. Seen together, these images preserve a portrait of the country while inviting viewers to reconsider how its history has been recorded.

items.title: Second court defeat for Trump's deep-sea mining ambitions
items.desc: Second judge rules against Trump administration's plans to lease areas of ocean floor and survey for mining.
items.text:
Campaigners worried the mining could impact sea turtles in the area
The Trump administration's plans to begin deep-sea mining in the Pacific have hit a second legal setback after a federal judge ruled plans to lease areas of sea-floor off the Northern Mariana Islands violated the Endangered Species Act (ESA).
The court's decision follows a similar ruling over a proposed lease sale off American Samoa.
Opposition groups who lodged the Northern Mariana Islands lawsuit said they were concerned deep-sea mining could cause long-term damage to the ocean ecosystem.
The US government has said it wants to start deep-sea mining to enable access to critical minerals and to counter China's growing influence over crucial components needed for electronics.
The administration had planned to put up for sale leases for the Northern Mariana Islands on 16 December 2026.
It is not clear what will happen next as the administration chose not to recognise the first court ruling and went ahead with the sale of two leases covering 13 million hectares (more than 30 million acres) off American Samoa.
Opponents have vowed to challenge that sale.
Ruling on the Northern Mariana Islands case, District judge Jill Aiko Otake said the defendants, the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), which provided the expert opinion behind the lease sales, and Howard Lutnick, who was named in his capacity as head of the department that oversees the agency, had failed to consider the potential effects that could follow once the leases were issued.
The ruling explained that while these leases would only authorise the leaseholder to conduct preliminary surveying activity, they might eventually allow the leaseholder to actually mine the ocean's floor.
The potential impact of that mining had not been addressed in the biodiversity assessment which was used to sign off the lease sales, the ruling said.
Using machines to mine for minerals in the deep ocean is highly controversial.
Some scientists have raised concerns that deep-sea mining could damage little-understood deep-ocean ecosystems, though industry supporters argue the environmental effects remain uncertain and require further study.
Deep-sea mining uses vacuum technology to suck up nodules from the muddy sediment. , external However, this process also removes organisms that grow on them, including corals and sponges, many of which cannot grow anywhere else.

In Japan, a nightclub traded loud music for books—for a day. A venue named SPREAD , located in Tokyo’s Shimokitazawa district, known for its alternative, bohemian vibes, hosted a “Book Rave.” The club turned the dance floor into a reading lounge with carpets where attendees could sit or lie down to read, as a DJ played ambient music to keep everyone focused. This isn’t a new trend taking over Japanese clubs; instead, it’s a unique event that has caught the world’s attention.
JUCY organized the event , and its Instagram bio simply reads, “We’re hosting Reading Parties at various locations in Tokyo.” The JUCY BOOK RAVE at SPREAD appears to be its first. And while it was held at a nightclub, the so-called “rave” ran from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. on a Saturday.
Instead of bringing their own books, attendees read the title recommended by the JUCY crew. The organizers also had some fiction titles available for sale. Attendees later discussed what they were reading and shared and traded books with others. According to the venue’ s event flyer, the ¥2,500 ($15.80) cover charge included two drinks and a copy of the book they read.
“This event is not a gathering where participants bring their own books to read; rather, it is an event where everyone reads a single work of literary fiction designated by the organizers,” the team said when promoting a second of these getogethers. “The book we plan to read for this event is Kohei Toyonaga’s Tsuki no Hashiri ya, Uma no Hashiri . We do not recommend participation if you have already read this book (though you are more than welcome to join if you’d like to reread it and share your thoughts with other participants.”
If you’re in the Tokyo area, follow JUCY on Instagram to stay up to date on its reading events.

items.desc: Minimalist Beach House Doubles as a Frame for the Ocean It Overlooks Casa Malonic, or Malonic House, is a recently completed residential project in the beach town of Zihuatanejo, Mexico. items.text:
Casa Malonic, or Malonic House, is a recently completed residential project in the beach town of Zihuatanejo, Mexico. But this is no ordinary beach house. Instead, it serves the striking oceanic landscape at its feet. Conceived by Mexico-based firm HW Studio , the entire design draws from two defining elements: the land it sits on and its colors, resulting in a construction that engages in a soft yet profound dialogue with the surrounding environment.
This gentle approach is almost a secret, for those who come across Casa Malonic from the street would see only a white mass wrapped in a single curved wall that almost signals brutalism . As the dwellers step inside, the entrance path leads to a circular courtyard where a soothing transition begins, as if the house sheds concrete layers to reveal its true nature. The walls then give way to a boundless view of the ocean and the surrounding landscape.
When first approaching the construction site, the architects were so fascinated by the area that they wanted to spotlight it. They made a point to honor the elements that predated the architecture: flora, fauna, topography, and sunlight. To do that, they reduced architecture to ground, roof, and shadow—its most basic elements. They found inspiration in an enramada , a simple shelter beneath a canopy that, even at its barest, can provide shade and protection from rain without enforcing a strict boundary.
This concept is what creates the most striking feature of Casa Malonic. Rather than providing just another floor-to-ceiling window or glass balcony to take in the beach landscape, the entire structure doubles as a frame for the horizon line. It’s also through this choice that the architects declare this view the spiritual heart of the house. To them, the horizon line is what makes the design possible; not the other way around.
Meant to be taken in as an all-encompassing habitat, the oceanic imagery is not limited to the views. The flooring imitates color and texture, evoking the sand below, as if establishing one continuous path to it. The white walls match the landscape by recalling the flowers of the nine Cacalosúchil trees that surround the house.
“The materiality does not seek to represent the landscape, but to establish a sensory continuity with it. Architecture is first experienced through the feet, before it is understood through the eyes,” writes HW Studio. “The project does not seek to reproduce nature, nor to disappear completely into it. items.text:
More than 400 years after the Pilgrims first explored the Cape Cod area, land belonging to Native Americans was returned to Indigenous ownership.
On October 30, The Nature Conservancy gave roughly 126 acres of salt marsh and natural habitat in Eastham, Massachusetts to the Native Land Conservancy, an Indigenous-led nonprofit based in Mashpee. The land sits right next to a 20.4-acre parcel the Conservancy bought earlier in the year for $3 million, linking them into a larger protected area that looks out over First Encounter Beach. ⁠
“This place holds so many stories that were buried and are ready to be unearthed,” Ramona Peters, founder and board president of the Native Land Conservancy and a member of the Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe, said in a published statement . “Long before the first encounter, Native people lived here and took care of this land.”
In December 1620, not long after the Mayflower arrived, an exploring party led by Myles Standish traded arrows and gunfire with Nauset warriors near what’s now called First Encounter Beach, named for the first hostile meeting between the Pilgrims and a native people.
The fight came after colonists had taken corn and disturbed graves. “Our ancestors weren’t just standing around. They were protecting their families, and taking care of this land lets us tell that story the right way,” R. Peters said.
The First Encounter with the Nauset on Cape Cod happened before the better-known harvest feast with the Wampanoag at Plymouth in 1621, but even that meeting lacked context. The Wampanoag were never invited; 90 warriors arrived and were invited to stay as an act of diplomacy after responding to celebratory musket fire from the colonists.
“The Thanksgiving holiday overlooks a myriad of sins. The backstory to colonization includes enslavement of Native men, the introduction of a devastating plague, the theft of corn and disturbance of graves of the Nauset people, and an alliance that robed the Wampanoag of their sovereignty and land,” Paula Peters, communications and program director at the Native Land Conservancy, said.
The salt marsh and nearby uplands also give a home to vulnerable animals, including diamondback terrapins that nest along the coastal bluffs. items.text:
Thanksgiving is a time for gathering, giving thanks, and remembering that joy is possible even when life has been hard. Few films capture that spirit better than Mission: JOY .
The documentary captures the unlikely, laughter-filled friendship between His Holiness the Dalai Lama and the late Archbishop Desmond Tutu, two Nobel Peace Prize laureates whose lives were defined by profound adversity – decades of exile for the Dalai Lama and the Archbishop’s long struggle with the violence and injustice of apartheid.
The two beloved figures sat together for five days in Dharamsala, India and mostly just cracked each other up. The result is the 90-minute documentary and the massive citizen-science project it inspired.
The film shows how their shared resilience, humor, and deep wisdom offer a practical path for anyone seeking to hold onto hope and agency when the world feels overwhelming. “People are always yearning to see deep connections. To see deep wisdom and to learn,” co-director and producer Peggy Callahan said. “And who doesn’t love to laugh through all of that at the same time?”
Despite extreme hardship, loss, and the weight of leading their people through some of the darkest chapters of the twentieth century, both men emerged as living proof that joy is not the absence of suffering but an inside job that can be cultivated even in the most troubled times.
The film’s central premise is that their joy was not naïve or accidental. As Callahan put it, “Joy is an inside job. No one can really take your joy. You can give it away. But it is an inside thing. You get to build that yourself.”
Callahan said watching the two Nobel Peace Prize laureates together reinforced what she had already concluded in her twenties: “The most interesting people have gotten their ass kicked at some point… they’ve gone through such traumatic times and through it all they found joy.”
The Dalai Lama and the late Archbishop Desmond Tutu spent as much time teasing one another, as they did discussing what they endured, with both men finding every opportunity to make each other smile.
“They were like little kids,” Callahan recalled, remembering a lunch when the cameras weren’t rolling when she had to remind the two icons to eat between laughs.

The Shanghai Grand Opera House , set along the Huangpu River, is more than a place to enjoy cultural performances. The striking building—designed by Norwegian architecture firm Snøhetta —features an epic, spiraling rooftop staircase that invites you to climb toward the clouds and enjoy spectacular views.
Spanning 1,569,991 square feet (146,786 square meters), the Opera House is built around three key ideas: movement, belonging, and experience. The design makes it easy for people to approach, enter, and explore the building, while creating an open, welcoming space for everyone. Every detail is designed with the visitor in mind, from the interior atmosphere to the journey audiences and performers take through the building.
The building’s sculptural form draws on the flow of the Huangpu River and the energy of the surrounding city, with the spiraling roof at its heart. It doubles as a stage, viewing deck, and gathering space that people can enjoy year-round. The huge spiral structure leads from the ground floor to the roof, offering views of the river and city skyline along the way and making the journey itself part of the experience. It also brings together a variety of public spaces, including restaurants, exhibition areas, education centers, and performance halls.
The opera house’s modern exterior reflects the contemporary performances and productions inside. The impressive building features three auditoriums hosting everything from traditional opera and classical music to experimental performances.

items.desc: The legendary character of the Silk Road was in full focus recently in Mongolia, where excavations of a nomad’s tomb unearthed objects all the way from Classical Rome. The tomb undoubtedly belonged to an elite individual from the Xiongnu people, a nomadic group that controlled large stretches of Central Asia, Mongolia, and Manchuria for some […] The post Roman Glass Among the Silk Road Treasures U
items.text:
The legendary character of the Silk Road was in full focus recently in Mongolia, where excavations of a nomad’s tomb unearthed objects all the way from Classical Rome.
The tomb undoubtedly belonged to an elite individual from the Xiongnu people, a nomadic group that controlled large stretches of Central Asia, Mongolia, and Manchuria for some 5 centuries.
In addition to a cup made from Roman glass, a gourd-shaped silver and crystal pendant, likely used to adorn a horse’s harness, closely resembles accessories found in tombs on the Korean Peninsula that date to the same period.
The discoveries highlight the Xiongnu’s role in a vast exchange network that linked these progenitors of the conquering Mongols to the Roman Empire, Han China, and the Korean Peninsula.
The Xiongnu’s role in East Asian history cannot be overstated, as much for what these nomadic horse archers did themselves as for what they brought out of their southern neighbors, the Han Chinese. To face down these ferocious warriors, the Chinese stamped their names into the history books with the building of the first Great Wall of China.
A need to secure horses to wage war on the Xiongnu required a stable route to Central Asia, which saw the establishment of Chinese control over the Gansu Corridor. This paved the way for the first iteration of the Silk Road out across the deserts and steppes of the Tarim Basin through to Modern-day Uzbekistan.
The Xiongnu existed as the most powerful confederation of nomadic tribes on the steppe for almost 5 centuries, a span of control unmatched until the rise of Genghis Khan over 1,000 years after their ultimate defeat by the Han.
Located in the Duurlig Nars burial ground, which contains around 300 graves, the newly excavated Tomb 160 is the largest Xiongnu tomb ever found in Mongolia to date. The exterior measures nearly 240 feet in length, but the interior chamber is surprisingly small and shallow, extending only about 50 feet deep.
This contrasts with deeper tombs in central Mongolia, suggesting changes in Xiongnu society during the late first and second centuries CE, a period when the empire was declining due to internal conflicts and pressure from the Han military.

The BBC explains that these comedic devices often depend on tone, social context, and subtle implications rather than obvious punchlines.
This is why a seemingly ordinary comment can become funny when it carries an underlying meaning that the listener is expected to recognize. A remark about terrible weather, for instance, can become amusing when delivered with exaggerated positivity, as both people understand the contradiction.

items.text:
Another of the infamous gentleman art thief “Erik the Belgian’s” heists have been solved.
For nearly half a century, a 13th-century carving of the Virgin Mary sat in a Spanish police database as an unsolved case.
The Romanesque sculpture vanished in 1979 from the Church of San Pedro de Meoz, a small parish in Navarre, swept up in a wave of church robberies that hit rural Spain hard where rich heritage was paired with almost no security.
The man blamed for it was René Alphonse van den Berghe, better known as Erik the Belgian, one of the most prolific art thieves in Modern history.
Now, at last, the piece is back where it belongs. Spain’s National Police announced its recovery from a collection in the United Kingdom, closing a trail that ran through Belgium, London and the Netherlands.
The sculpture is a seated walnut-wood Virgin, still carrying traces of its original gilding and polychrome, measuring 54 centimeters tall and holding the figure of the Christ Child—though she’s missing both forearms. Small enough to wrap in a blanket, valuable enough to disappear into the antiques trade for decades, that combination made her exactly Erik’s type.
A veritable manifestation of the fictional Arsène Lupin, Van den Berghe (1940–2020) robbed churches and monasteries across sparsely populated parts of his adopted country of Spain and elsewhere in Europe.
Thousands of crimes have been attributed to him, much of it involving medieval sacred art. He was also a painter and a forger, and in his later years leaned hard on his reputation as a “gentleman thief,” giving interviews, recounting heists, and even helping recover some of his own marks.
In 2023, GNN reported that a two-foot by two-foot square cut away from the bottom left corner of a 17th-century tapestry was recovered with the help of none other than the man who had held the scissors: The Belgian.
Van den Berghe’s most famous job was the 1980 theft of the silver Ark of Sant Martirià from the monastery of Sant Esteve de Banyoles in Girona, the prized reliquary of the town’s patron saint forged from silver in the 15th century.
The investigation into the Virgin Mary work was restarted in April after authorities got a useful lead, and quickly confirmed a long-suspected method of Erik: the loot went out by road to countries with hungrier art and antiques markets.

items.title: Rare turtles found inside baggage at Amsterdam airport
items.desc: The endangered reptiles were bound with duct tape to prevent them moving, officials say.
items.text:
An official holds one of the seized Vallarta mud turtles - they are now receiving care at a specialised sanctuary
Twenty-six "very rare" turtles have been seized from a traveller's checked baggage at Amsterdam's Schiphol airport, a Dutch government agency has said.
The Netherlands Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority (NVWA) said a man flying from Mexico to Hong Kong via the airport was arrested on Saturday after the Vallarta mud turtles were found by customs officers.
The endangered species, thought to be the smallest freshwater turtles in the world with a maximum length of about 10cm (4in), were wrapped in duct tape to prevent them from moving.
The NVWA said they were "presumably stolen" from the wild in their native Mexico.
It said most of the turtles were found in a box with a toy car, while the others were in a closed sock inside a suitcase.
The arrested man remains in custody and an investigation is under way.
Meanwhile, the turtles are receiving care at a "specialised sanctuary", the NVWA said.
In 2025, the US NGO Turtle Island estimated that no more than 300 Vallarta mud turtles existed in the wild.
They are listed as critically endangered on a list published by the International Union for Conservation of Nature.
According to environmental news outlet Mongabay, a Vallarta mud turtle can sell for $10,000 (£7,500) or more on the black market in Asia.
Other cases of live turtles being smuggled to Hong Kong have been reported this year.
In October, customs authorities in Hong Kong were reported to have seized eight turtles , external that were thought to be endangered. The reptiles had an estimated market value of about $54,000.
Three months prior, Hong Kong customs detected two separate smuggling cases , external . Some 42 live turtles, with a total estimated market value of $210,000 were seized.

items.desc: New Study Finds That Dogs May Understand Our Language in More Ways Than We Thought We’ve always known dogs are smart, but a new study in Science reveals they may process human speech in ways even more sophisticated than we thought. items.text:
We’ve always known dogs are smart , but a new study in Science reveals they may process human speech in ways even more sophisticated than we thought .
Across many languages, consonants carry more significance than vowels, which generally convey less information about the word being spoken. As a result, human brains have learned to recognize and rely heavily on consonant patterns when listening to speech. Until now, no other non-human species had been shown to do the same thing.
Through the use of electroencephalography, or EEG, a noninvasive test that measures electrical activity in the brain, researchers found that dogs may also display this same consonant bias. This means that while they may not understand the meaning of the words we are saying, their brains can still pick out patterns in human speech in a way surprisingly similar to ours.
The scientists involved in the study still aren’t sure exactly why dogs have developed this ability. It could have something to do with their long history of living alongside humans and regularly hearing us speak, or it could point to a more general ability to recognize sound patterns that existed long before dogs were domesticated. For now, researchers say there isn’t enough evidence to know for sure.
The study does not mean that dogs know what the words humans use actually mean. Instead, it shows that their brains can seek out and favor consonant patterns. What makes this even more interesting is that vowels carry more acoustic energy, meaning they naturally stand out more when we hear them. Yet the dogs’ brains still seemed to favor the quieter consonants, suggesting that they weren’t simply paying attention to the loudest sounds.
To test this, researchers played recordings of meaningless, three-syllable words to 20 adult dogs while electrodes on their heads measured brain activity. Researchers then performed the same experiment with 20 human adults. The recordings played continuously, without pauses telling the dogs or humans where one made-up word ended and another began. In one version, repeated consonant patterns helped separate the stream of syllables into words. In another, the same thing was done using vowels instead. A third recording mixed everything up completely, leaving no repeating pattern for either group to recognize.

Trialed over 4 years in […] The post Major Succ
items.text:
A major success in population-scale control of mosquito-borne viruses comes now from Brazil, where schoolchildren are enjoying a 68% lower risk of such diseases.
The trial tested the largely-proven method of releasing mosquitoes infected with Wolbachia bacteria, which inhibits the insect’s ability to spread viruses like dengue, Zika, and chikungunya.
Trialed over 4 years in Belo Horizonte, the success overlapped with the largest outbreak of dengue fever ever recorded in Brazil, demonstrating the urgent need for greater mosquito control in the tropics.
“The intervention substantially reduced dengue infections during Brazil’s largest recorded outbreak, demonstrating its potential to protect communities even under conditions of intense transmission,” states Derek Cummings, PhD, co-principal investigator of the trial and Bloomberg Distinguished Professor at Johns Hopkins University, one of the institutions that participated.
Called the EVITA dengue trial, the international team set out to test a locally-adapted version of the wMel strain of Wolbachia for use in inhibiting viral transmission from Aedes aegypti mosquitoes.
wMel is the most commonly-used strain of Wolbachia, with the ‘Mel’ referring to the fruit fly species from which Wolbachia was first isolated. wMel-infected mosquitoes pass the bacteria to their offspring, thereby inhibiting disease transmission on a generational scale.
EVITA included 58 school-defined geographic clusters in Belo Horizonte, with 29 clusters assigned to receive releases of wMel mosquitoes in addition to standard vector-control measures, and 29 clusters assigned to standard vector control alone, such as insecticidal sprays and mosquito source reduction.
The randomized-controlled trial released Wolbachia-infected mosquitoes from January 2021 through May 2022. It involved 5,757 school children, ages 6 to 11. The results were presented on Saturday at the American Society of Tropical Medicine & Hygiene annual meeting in National Harbor, Maryland.

items.desc: History is serious business, and reading about past events can get pretty grim pretty quickly. To show you the past in a different — slightly sarcastic and slightly funny — light, we have collected the most hilarious memes and tweets from around the internet. These posts don’t spare even the darkest moments or the most famous historical figures.
items.text:
It might seem strange to turn historical events and figures into memes, especially when the topics are so grim. Wars and destruction are about as far from funny as you can get. Still, for many people online, these exact subjects make up a popular type of comedy.
That’s because dark humor helps some people process events that would otherwise feel way too painful or upsetting. Laughing is a classic way to handle stress, even if not every joke lands well.
Making jokes about serious subjects does not always mean a person lacks empathy. In fact, experts say the exact opposite might be true.
For many people, sharing a meme is simply a way to calm down and cope with a scary world. “For some people, using memes to convey information can add both meaning and levity to very threatening situations,” says Carla Manly, PhD, a clinical psychologist.
“By adding a dose of humor, more comical memes downplay the severity of crises. For example, a humorous meme oriented toward being drafted may, at its foundation, be based on a fear of being drafted. In such cases, memes may offer a dose of cathartic psychological relief.”
A Penn State study showed that simply scrolling through memes—even ones about big, stressful events like COVID-19—lifts your mood and helps you feel more ready to tackle daily stress.
Internet jokes also help people deal with deeper struggles. Research shows that those with anxiety often use memes to manage their feelings. In the same way, people facing depression tend to find jokes about their condition much funnier and easier to relate to than others do.
History memes not only make you laugh, but they can also help you learn. One study found that history memes led to a 22.8% boost in students' interest in learning about the past.
Even better, 76.85% of the students surveyed agreed that these funny posts helped them hit their learning goals. The researchers noted that based on Edgar Dale’s cone theory, history memes can even improve how well we remember facts from the past by up to 30%.

items.text:
What began as an 11-year-old boy’s promise to his mother has launched ‘Thanksgiving Heroes,’ a nationwide effort to bring holiday meals to those in need. This year, they will feed 3,600 families in Utah alone.
Rob Adams, founder of Thanksgiving Heroes , grew up as the oldest of six children in South Texas. For a stretch of his childhood, the family lived out of their pickup truck in Porter, an unincorporated area near Houston. They had little clothing and often relied on school lunches as the one guaranteed meal of the day. Adams has said he still remembers being a happy, loved child, but the hardship was real.
One Christmas, a neighboring family—the Christiansons—drove the Adams family about 12 miles to their home in Kingwood. The house was picture-perfect, complete with a Christmas tree. The Christiansons were leaving for the holidays and invited the Adams family to stay while they were gone.
They left the refrigerator fully stocked with turkey, pumpkin pie, and other food, with presents for the children under the tree. The gesture of unconditional kindness left a lasting mark. At 11, Adams told his mother that one day, when he was “rich,” which at the time simply meant not sleeping in their car, he would pay it forward. “I feel like I owe this to another family because someone was so kind to me,” Adams said.
Years later, as his mother faced a brain-cancer diagnosis, she reminded him of that childhood vow and urged him to follow through. That push led Adams to launch Thanksgiving Heroes.
Adams set a modest goal the first year: feed 10 families. Instead, Thanksgiving Heroes provided meals to about 755 families. This year, the group aims to reach 3,600 families across Utah , but the fulfillment of Adams’ promise extends beyond state lines.
Thanksgiving Heroes has grown into a national network of local affiliates that together have served more than 29,000 families. While the Utah chapter remains the largest—having provided meals to nearly 20,000 families since 2015—the model has spread through independent affiliates that receive support from the parent foundation.
Established chapters now operate in Cleveland, Ohio (more than 6,600 families since 2020) and Las Vegas (hundreds of families since 2021), while newer affiliates have launched in Phoenix, Orange County, California, Stark County, Ohio, and New Haven, Connecticut. items.text:
The coconut palm is often called the Tree of 1,000 Uses, though ‘school tuition voucher’ is not typically one of those 1,000.
Yet the Faith Christian Academy in Micronesia is, in fact, accepting coconuts in lieu of tuition costs—to help ease the financial burden on families while making use of the ubiquitous fruits that pile up all around.
The Academy’s new tuition plan actually clears 2 hurdles in 1 leap. Students can easily afford tuition while sparing themselves the dangers and toil of fishing to make money. On the other, the coconuts are used by the Academy to rebuild Yap Island’s once-flourishing coconut oil industry.
“Yap is beautiful, but cash is hard to come by,” says Paul Zimmer, founder and CEO of 3 different organizations working on Yap Island, including the Academy. “Almost every family lives off the land and sea. 95% of households grow crops, 88% fish, and 78% grow coconuts, nearly all for their own table.”
“We asked a simple question: what if the thing Yap has in abundance could help pay for the thing families want most for their kids?”
Zimmer would go on to tell GNN that only one-third of all islanders had cash-paying work, most of which was through the government. The notion of a local economy is almost a dream. Everything needed that can’t be grown is imported, and virtually nothing is exported. That wasn’t always the case, however.
According to Zimmer, this island state within the Federated States of Micronesia used to be a large exporter of virgin coconut oil, but slowing exports through the ’90s stopped entirely by the mid-2000s “because prices were low, shipping was poor, and the palms were aging.”
Though the market was gone, the coconuts kept on growing. At the same time, a decade of balancing the books at Faith Christian Academy (FCA) demonstrated that students would often have to work themselves to the bone to afford the tuition costs.
At times, this would involve dangerous nighttime fishing, while at other times it meant double shifts at work for low-wage earners: like the father of Shayalynn, whose family is from the outer island of Ifaluk, but who has attended FCA since 2017.
“I felt relieved and happy about it because my dad didn’t have to work a lot for my tuition,” she said, remembering when she first heard about the coconuts, “The first year that I started in FCA in 2017, he had to work double shifts just to be able to pay for my tuition, the food on the table, and the clothes that I had to wear to school.”

items.title: New satellite data shows how fast some African cities are sinking
items.desc: Cities including Lagos and Alexandria are sinking faster than previously thought, a new study shows.
items.text:
Four million people in Lagos, Nigeria may be exposed to extreme sea levels by the end of the century, a new study says
Some of Africa's largest cities are sinking faster than previously thought, new research shows.
Scientists used radar imagery from the European Space Agency's Sentinel-1 satellites to map how much the land beneath 20 African coastal cities had moved.
The study found that some cities - including Lagos in Nigeria and Alexandria in Egypt - were sinking much faster than previously estimated in 2021 by the UN's climate body, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).
While some causes of this sinking, or subsidence, are natural, many are the result of human activities, such as the extraction of groundwater from underneath the Earth's surface.
Lead author Oluwaseyi Dasho said the effects of subsidence "are often invisible in everyday life, but over decades they can substantially increase flood exposure".
This is because when the ground sinks it becomes lower relative to the ocean and adds to the risk of the sea level rises caused by climate change .
Seven million people, one billion buildings and $180bn (£137bn) of assets could be at flood risk by 2050, the paper estimated.
In the past, a lack of monitoring stations has prevented scientists from obtaining up-to-date localised information on subsidence in Africa, Dasho said.
But by using satellite data, the researchers from Virginia Tech were able to detect land movements as small as 1mm per year.
Senior author Manoochehr Shirzaei said Sentinel-1 satellites flew over the same region of the Earth every six to 12 days.
"[The satellite] transmits the radar signal, which hits the ground and bounces back to the satellite," the geosciences professor explained. This process is then repeated on "many revisits".
The time between sending the signal and receiving it back is recorded, with changes in this value over time revealing how much the land has moved.
More of Alexandria could be exposed to flooding than previously thought, the research says
The ground under Alexandria and Lagos was found to have sunk an average of 6mm and 5mm per year respectively.
If this rate continued, sea levels around Alexandria would rise 36% more by 2050 than the IPCC predicted , external , under the middle estimates for how much planet-warming emissions will increase.
Luanda in Angola has also sunk significantly, but other cities such as Durban in South Africa have remained stable or even risen slightly.

items.text:
105 years ago today, Rued Langgaard’s “ Music of the Spheres ” (Sfærernes Musik) premiered at Konzerthaus in Karlsruhe, Germany. Replicating a variety of outer spatial senses through the careful and considered multi-movement work, it includes several methods of orchestral composition well ahead of its time. Several of the movements project the sense of vast space and distance, particularly through the positioning of a small, secondary orchestra off stage. READ more about the work, and listen to it… (1921)
The piece was inspired by a line from a Danish poem translated as, “the stars seem to twinkle kindly at us, yet the writing of the stars is cold and merciless.” Langgard vacates much of the middle tonal range in favor of extreme basso and treble clusters. This lack of depth seems to mimic outer space.
Strings repeatedly stay on single notes, rising and falling in volume as if capturing the orbit of a celestial body. By playing directly on the piano strings, something that had never been done before in orchestra, the musicians plunk out little dampened lights in the darkness of the composition’s vast spaces. It concludes with a sort of end times-like fury, before falling away again to angelic choir and distance.
The premiere was a success, but the following year it received a more lukewarm reception when performed in Berlin. It was not performed again until 1968, where a performance in Stockholm with the Royal Stockholm Philharmonic Orchestra, conducted by Sergiu Comissiona, ignited a renaissance for Langgaard’s music.
15 years ago today, the Mars Science Laboratory launched from Earth carrying the Curiosity Rover with the objectives including the investigation of Mars’ habitability, studying its climate and geology, and collecting data for a human mission to Mars. Curiosity is about twice as long and five times as heavy as previous Martian rovers Spirit and Opportunity, and carries over ten times the mass of scientific instruments.
In an article on the five most important discoveries made by Curiosity’s decade of exploring Gale Crater and Mount Sharp, NASA program scientists agree that the detection of organic molecules with Curiosity’s Sample Analysis at Mars (SAM) instrument suite is one of the biggest.

items.title: Hundreds of thousands still without power a day after US slammed with Thanksgiving storms
items.desc: Pennsylvania and neighbouring states remained badly affected on Friday after both coasts were lashed with wind and rain.
items.text:
Watch: Severe Thanksgiving storms leave roads flooded and trees fallen
More than 260,000 people remain without power after severe weather hit both coasts of the United States during the Thanksgiving holiday.
Eastern areas were lashed on Thursday by a powerful storm which brought high winds, heavy rain and coastal flooding. Pennsylvania remained the state worst hit by power cuts early on Friday, according to monitoring site Poweroutage.us.
Conditions are now improving, though forecasters caution that it will take some time. The West Coast also was affected by its own storms.
Flight disruption persisted, too, with hundreds more delays and cancellations reported on Friday - another busy travel day.
More than 3,400 flights within, into, or out of the US were delayed and nearly 670 cancelled on Friday.
On Thanksgiving, more than 2,500 US flights were delayed and more than 450 were cancelled, according to Flightaware.com. One passenger told the BBC he had been stuck at New York's LaGuardia Airport for 13 hours while trying to fly to see friends in Chicago for Thanksgiving.
Beyond the travel disruption, impacts were widespread across the East Coast, and US President Donald Trump said he would consider releasing emergency funds.
Bridges closed in Maryland due to severe winds, while waves battered beaches in Delaware as water seeped onto the boardwalk. On the wettest Thanksgiving on record in Washington, tidal waters surged and soaked runways at Reagan Washington National Airport.
A powerful coastal storm flooded the streets of Ocean City, New Jersey on Thanksgiving
Parts of some states declared states of emergency overnight between Thursday and Friday, including New York.
Nearly 2in (5cm) of rain fell on New York City's iconic Central Park, making it the wettest Thanksgiving on record at that site as well, according to preliminary data , external from the NWS.
Organisers of the city's annual Macy's Thanksgiving parade have also pushed back the event to Saturday - marking the event's first postponement in its 100-year history.
In neighbouring New Jersey, there were multiple reports of closed roads and bridges, and images of floodwater blanketing city streets. Coastal flood warnings persisted for parts of New Jersey through the evening on Friday.
"This is wild," an Ocean City, New Jersey-based blogger said in a video , external posted on social media, as he waded through water splashing above his waist.

items.title: The rising cost of putting food on the table in India
items.desc: India's food inflation is broadening, squeezing household budgets.
items.text:
As food inflation rises, vegetables are becoming an increasingly expensive part of the household budget
India's inflation is rising again. And the biggest worry is what's happening to food prices.
The latest government data , external shows retail inflation climbed to 6.09% in October, up from 5.54% in September.
But look more closely at food inflation. It has surged to 8.94%.
The squeeze was sharper in rural India, where food inflation was 9.09%, compared with 8.68% in urban areas.
In other words, food prices are rising considerably faster than the overall rate of inflation.
Food inflation this year has been driven by a combination of weather disruptions, supply shortages and rising input costs, say economists.
With nearly 60% of its farmland dependent on rainfall , external , India remains acutely vulnerable to the vagaries of the monsoon. This year, the southwest monsoon was 13% below normal and unevenly distributed, while intensifying El Niño conditions have heightened risks to farm production.
Onion prices have surged, adding to the pressure on household food budgets
A survey by polling agency LocalCircles found that six in 10 consumers say household essentials cost them over 20% more each month than a year ago, prompting calls for government intervention.
Rising prices are also forcing cutbacks: 74% are curbing discretionary spending on eating out, shopping and entertainment, while half are buying smaller quantities of essentials.
Food accounts for a smaller share of Indian household spending than it once did, but remains the biggest driver of inflation, with significant economic, social and political consequences.
In India's latest consumer price index, food and beverages account for 36.75% of the basket of goods and services used to measure inflation.
That is down sharply from 45.86% under the previous series, reflecting changing consumption patterns as Indians spend more on services, transport, healthcare, education and other non-food items.
Yet a sharp increase in food prices can move the overall inflation rate significantly, while disproportionately affecting people whose incomes leave little room for adjustment.
"Adjustability for a poor country like India is significantly lower," says Rajeswari Sengupta, an associate professor of economics at Mumbai-based Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, pointing to the fact that a substantial proportion of household income is still spent on food.

items.text:
121 years ago today, American photographer Alfred Stieglitz opened the Little Galleries of the Photo-Secession at 291 Fifth Avenue in NYC. This small gallery helped bring art photography to the same stature in America as painting and sculpture, exhibiting famous early photographers like Edward Steichen, Alvin Langdon Coburn, Gertrude Käsebier, and Clarence H. White. But, it also being an avantgarde gallery space, 291 also hosted the first solo US exhibitions of painters and sculptors like Pablo Picasso, Henri Matisse, and Paul Cezanne. READ more about this little known American art landmark… (1905)
Alfred Stieglitz believed that photography could share space with fine art, and certainly the photo camera at the time produced images that didn’t have so much more resolution than what could be achieved by a determined painter. To that end, and at the urging of his friends in the photography world of New York City at the turn of the century, on December 1901, Stieglitz put on his first photography exposition, launched the first all-photography magazine in 1903, and opened the Little Galleries in 1905.
The gallery became an instant success, with almost fifteen thousand visitors during its first season and, more importantly, print sales that totaled nearly $2,800. The opening show was followed by an exhibition of photographers from France, then 5 more from American photographers, one for British, and one for Germans and Austrians.
Its success wavered over the decades, during which time American artist Georgia O’Keeffe, whom Stieglitz married, was exhibited many times alongside the other fine painters mentioned above.
42 years ago today, three dozen musicians from the UK gathered in a London studio to record Do They Know It’s Christmas for the sole purpose of raising money to send food to starving families in Ethiopia. Dreamed up and written by Bob Geldof, music sales for Band Aid , the world’s first charity super-group, raised $14 million. Watch their music video below, starring a young Phil Collins, Sting, Paul McCartney, and Bono.
The updated 2014 version of the song, by Band-Aid 30 , raised money for the Ebola crisis. Geldof, who later created Live Aid, updated his song “Do They Know…” to describe the Ebola epidemic (see the video on YouTube ).
